title: Box Office Triumph: ‘Clayface’ Debuts at No. 1 with $10.4 M, ‘You Can See Everything’ Adds $6.14 M Friday
body:
The new DC horror‑action film *Clayface* opened this weekend atop the U.S. box office, pulling in $10.4 million on its first day and $28.7 million over the opening weekend. The figure is especially striking given the character’s relative obscurity compared with marquee names such as Superman or Wonder Woman. The movie’s gritty, blood‑soaked origin story for the shape‑shifting Batman villain resonated with genre‑hungry moviegoers, while a surprise Friday performer, the Chinese thriller *You Can See Everything*, added another $6.14 million to the day’s tally, underscoring the growing clout of international titles in the domestic market.

*Clayface*—directed by veteran horror filmmaker Gregor K. Miller—leans heavily into practical effects and a visceral aesthetic, a creative choice that appears to have paid off. The film follows the tragic transformation of scientist Basil Karlo, whose experimental serum turns him into a malleable, murderous entity capable of assuming any form. Critics have highlighted the movie’s effective blend of body‑horror set pieces and a surprisingly sympathetic core, allowing it to stand out in a crowded superhero slate that has leaned toward glossy spectacle in recent years. Its $10.4 million debut eclipsed the opening of many mid‑budget genre entries and placed it ahead of the $9.8 million earned by the animated family film *The Little Mermaid* in its second weekend, signaling a robust appetite for darker, more adult‑oriented comic adaptations.

Industry analysts point to several factors behind the strong performance. First, the timing of the release—mid‑October, just before Halloween—provided a natural audience boost for horror‑themed fare. Second, the film benefited from a strategic marketing push that highlighted its practical makeup and creature effects, appealing to both longtime comic fans and horror aficionados. Third, the absence of direct competition from other major releases allowed *Clayface* to dominate multiplex screens, especially in urban markets where the DC fan base is concentrated. The film’s success also illustrates the viability of lower‑budget, high‑concept superhero projects in an era where studios are increasingly cautious about ballooning production costs.

The Friday surprise, *You Can See Everything*, a Chinese psychological thriller that opened in limited release across select U.S. cities, contributed $6.14 million to the day’s total—a notable achievement for a non‑English language film without a massive promotional budget. Its performance reflects a broader trend of international titles making inroads into the American box office, driven by streaming platforms that have familiarized U.S. audiences with foreign narratives and by the growing demographic of Asian‑American moviegoers. Distributors are now more willing to give such films a wider theatrical rollout, betting on niche appeal and word‑of‑mouth buzz rather than massive ad spends.

While *Clayface*’s numbers are impressive, they also raise questions about the future direction of DC’s cinematic strategy. The studio has been experimenting with a diversified slate that includes family‑friendly fare, gritty standalone films, and now horror‑centric entries. If the modest budget—estimated at roughly $30 million—translates into a healthy profit margin, Warner Bros. Discovery may greenlight additional genre‑bending projects that explore lesser‑known corners of the DC universe. Such a move could help the brand avoid the fatigue that sometimes accompanies overexposure of its flagship heroes, while also attracting a more adult demographic that has drifted toward streaming services for mature content.

Looking ahead, the weekend’s box office results suggest a shifting landscape where both niche superhero stories and foreign thrillers can compete for mainstream attention. As *Clayface* settles into its second week, its performance will be closely watched as a barometer for the profitability of horror‑infused comic adaptations. Meanwhile, the unexpected strength of *You Can See Everything* may encourage distributors to pursue broader theatrical releases for select international titles, further diversifying the American moviegoing experience. In an industry still adjusting to post‑pandemic habits, the success of these two very different films underscores the audience’s appetite for fresh, daring storytelling—whether it comes from Gotham’s darkest corners or across the Pacific.
